content: A preand postnatal developmental toxicity study was conducted in rats to evaluate the effects of esomeprazole magnesium on bone development. The study involved oral doses ranging from 14 to 280 mg/kg/day, which correspond to approximately 3.4 to 57 times the oral human dose of 40 mg based on body surface area. Neonatal and early postnatal survival (from birth to weaning) was reduced at doses equal to or greater than 138 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 33 times the human oral dose of 40 mg based on body surface area. At doses equal to or greater than 69 mg/kg/day (approximately 16.8 times the human oral dose of 40 mg), reductions in body weight and body weight gain were observed. Additionally, neurobehavioral and general developmental delays were evident during the immediate post-weaning period. Doses equal to or greater than 14 mg/kg/day (approximately 3.4 times the human oral dose of 40 mg) resulted in decreased femur length, width, and cortical bone thickness. There was also a reduction in the thickness of the tibial growth plate and minimal to mild bone marrow hypocellularity. Physeal dysplasia in the femur was observed in the offspring of rats treated with oral doses of esomeprazole magnesium at doses equal to or greater than 138 mg/kg/day (approximately 33.6 times the human oral dose of 40 mg). Effects on maternal bone were noted in pregnant and lactating rats when esomeprazole magnesium was administered at oral doses ranging from 14 to 280 mg/kg/day (approximately 3.4 to 57 times the human oral dose of 40 mg). When rats were dosed from gestational day 7 through weaning on postnatal day 21, a statistically significant decrease in maternal femur weight of up to 14% (compared to placebo treatment) was observed at doses equal to or greater than 138 mg/kg/day (approximately 33.6 times the human oral dose of 40 mg). A similar preand postnatal developmental study using esomeprazole strontium (at equimolar doses to the esomeprazole magnesium study) produced comparable results in dams and pups. There is no guidance from the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) on the use of esomeprazole sodium in pregnant women. The FDA has not provided guidance on the use of esomeprazole sodium during labor and delivery. Esomeprazole is likely present in human milk. Limited data suggest that maternal doses of omeprazole (20 mg daily) result in low levels in human milk. Caution is advised when administering esomeprazole sodium to nursing women. The safety and effectiveness of esomeprazole sodium for injection have been established in pediatric patients aged 1 month to 17 years for the short-term treatment of GERD with erosive esophagitis. However, its effectiveness has not been established in patients less than 1 month of age. For pediatric patients aged 1 month to 17 years, the use of esomeprazole sodium for injection for short-term treatment of GERD with erosive esophagitis is supported by pharmacokinetic (PK) studies, population PK modeling comparing adult and pediatric data, and pharmacodynamic results from both adult and pediatric studies. These findings are consistent with data included in the approved labeling for adults. In neonates (0 to 1 month of age), following administration of esomeprazole sodium, the geometric mean clearance (CL) was 0.17 L/h/kg (range: 0.04 to 0.32 L/h/kg). The safety and effectiveness of esomeprazole sodium in neonates have not been established. In a juvenile rat toxicity study, esomeprazole was administered with both magnesium and strontium salts at oral doses approximately 34 to 57 times the daily human dose of 40 mg based on body surface area. Increased mortality was observed at the highest dose, and decreases in body weight, body weight gain, femur weight, femur length, and overall growth were noted at all doses. In clinical trials, 1,459 patients aged 65 to 74 years and 354 patients aged 75 years or older received oral esomeprazole (NEXIUM). No overall differences in safety and efficacy were observed between elderly and younger patients. However, greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. The FDA has not provided specific guidance on the use of esomeprazole sodium with respect to gender, race, renal impairment, or immunocompromised patients. For adult patients with GERD, no dosage adjustment is necessary in those with mild to moderate hepatic insufficiency (Child-Pugh Classes A and B). For patients with severe hepatic insufficiency (Child-Pugh Class C), a dose of 20 mg once daily should not be exceeded. In cases of bleeding gastric or duodenal ulcers with liver impairment, no adjustment of the initial esomeprazole 80 mg infusion is required. However, for patients with severe liver impairment, a maximum continuous infusion rate of 4 mg/h should not be exceeded. There is no FDA guidance on the use of esomeprazole sodium in women of reproductive potential or males. The reconstituted solution of esomeprazole sodium should be stored at room temperature (up to 30°C or 86°F) and administered within 12 hours after reconstitution. If 5% Dextrose Injection is used, administration should occur within 6 hours. Refrigeration is not required. For intravenous injection in adults, the freeze-dried powder should be reconstituted with 5 mL of 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, and administered over no less than 3 minutes. For pediatric patients, intravenous infusion should be administered over 10 to 30 minutes, with the solution prepared by reconstituting the vial contents with 5 mL of 0.9% Sodium Chloride Injection, USP, Lactated Ringer’s Injection, USP, or 5% Dextrose Injection, USP, and further diluting to a final volume of 50 mL.
